newsitem.title: INDIA: Bronchitis continues to dog Mother Teresa.
newsitem.headline: Bronchitis continues to dog Mother Teresa.

text.p: Mother Teresa's doctors said on Thursday that nagging respiratory disease is continuing to delay her recovery from recent heart surgery.

"The pulmonary problem does not allow us to fully (improve) her overall condition," a panel of doctors treating the revered, 86-year-old missionary at Calcutta's B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre said in a regular update on her condition.
Last month the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner underwent surgery to clear two blocked coronary arteries. She had similar surgery in 1991 in the United States and in 1993 at the Birla clinic.

Dr Patricia Aubanel, an American member of the medical panel, this week said Mother Teresa had been dogged by lung disease since childhood and had suffered from bronchitis, an inflammation of the lining of the bronchial tubes, for the past two months.
Clinic officials said the nun had suffered some chest pain due to the bronchitis early on Thursday, but had recovered to eat her breakfast and say her prayers.
"The chest pain is now all right. The discomfort was because of pulmonary infection," A.K. Chatterjee, an administrator at the clinic, told reporters.
Mother Teresa was in a subdued mood, Chatterjee said. "Today she is not talking, most of the time she is quiet," he said.
However, she managed to meet with colleagues from her Missionaries of Charity religious order.

On Wednesday, doctors gave her a mild electric shock to correct an irregular heart beat. Afterwards they said the procedure, during which Mother Teresa remained conscious but under sedation, was a success.
But the eight-member team of doctors said on Thursday that the Roman Catholic nun's health remained at risk. They said the first 48 hours after the procedure were crucial.
"Mother Teresa is not stable as yet. We hope that her normal rhythm is a way to help us accomplish this, but it is (too) early to say," the latest update said.
The revered missionary has been pressing doctors to let her return to her religious order to resume her work with the sick and dying, for which she has been dubbed "Saint of the Gutters".
But doctors have cautioned that her recovery will be slow and she might never be as active as before.
